content: The Ernst & Young study from 2006 estimated the indirect economic impact of beer-related employment in the European Union by applying a multiplier of 50% to the initial indirect impact. This adjustment accounted for secondary economic effects, which added approximately 120,000 jobs to their overall estimate of beer-attributable employment in the EU. However, no alternative estimates have been conducted to allow for direct comparisons regarding alcohol-related employment. Arthur Andersen Economic Consulting, in a 1993 analysis of tobacco-related employment, noted that many jobs attributed to the tobacco industry are not directly involved in tobacco production, supply, or services. These jobs are unrelated to tobacco in any significant way. This observation highlights the complexity of attributing employment to specific industries. When examining the potential economic effects of reduced alcohol consumption, it is evident that some sectors may benefit while others may experience losses due to shifts in consumer spending. However, these adjustments are likely to be distributed across the broader economy, unlike the concentrated nature of alcohol sales in specific retail sectors. As a result, while these induced estimates are considered accurate, they are not deemed critical for policymaking. The largest number of jobs dependent on alcohol revenues are found in the hospitality sector, including hotels, restaurants, and catering (HoReCa), which primarily employs low-skilled workers. Conversely, other sectors, such as agriculture and specialized retail, may face varying degrees of difficulty in adjusting to changes in alcohol consumption. For example, vine growers may encounter more challenges than barley farmers due to the specialized nature of their production. In the long term, economists generally expect that a decline in alcohol consumption will have a negligible net effect on overall employment. This is because reduced spending on alcohol is likely to be redirected toward other goods and services, creating jobs in other areas of the economy. However, the adjustment costs for sectors directly involved in alcohol production may vary depending on the pace of consumption decline and the extent to which production is export-oriented. Alcohol consumption imposes significant societal costs, including healthcare expenses, law enforcement costs (such as courts and prisons), crime prevention, property damage, traffic accidents, workplace productivity losses, unemployment, and premature mortality. In some countries, alcohol is also linked to the economic burden of HIV/AIDS. Implementing effective alcohol policies, such as taxation and pricing strategies, can reduce these societal costs, often outweighing any potential economic disadvantages associated with such policies. Cost-effectiveness studies have shown that taxation is one of the most effective strategies for reducing alcohol-related harm, particularly in regions with a high prevalence of heavy drinking. For example, increasing alcohol taxation by 50% has been found to avert disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) at a relatively low cost. Other strategies, such as advertising bans and restricted access to alcohol outlets, are also cost-effective, while interventions like random breath testing tend to have higher costs per DALY averted. Dedicated taxes on alcohol, where a portion of the revenue is earmarked for health promotion and harm prevention activities, have been successfully implemented in several countries. For instance, Thailand’s ThaiHealth foundation is funded by a 2% surcharge on alcohol and tobacco excise taxes, providing sustainable financial support for health promotion initiatives. This model has proven effective in enhancing public health efforts and serves as an example of how earmarked taxes can be used to address alcohol-related harms. In conclusion, while alcohol consumption contributes to employment in certain sectors, its societal costs are substantial. Effective alcohol control policies, including taxation and pricing strategies, can reduce these costs and improve public health outcomes. Earmarking alcohol tax revenues for health promotion activities offers a sustainable approach to addressing alcohol-related harms while supporting broader public health goals.
